subject: Computer Science
summary: Covers the software life cycle and process models (waterfall, prototype, incremental, RAD, spiral, agile), requirements and SRS, design quality (cohesion, coupling, partitioning), testing techniques and cyclomatic complexity, estimation (FP, COCOMO, PERT/CPM) and maintenance, quality and reliability. DSSSB regularly asks model names, cohesion/coupling definitions, testing terms, full forms (CASE, SQA, MTTF, ROCOF) and formula-based questions.

sections.heading: Software, software engineering and the SDLC
sections.body:
**Software engineering** is the systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software (IEEE). Software differs from hardware: it is **developed, not manufactured**, and it **does not wear out** but deteriorates because of changes (Pressman).

The **Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)** is the set of phases a product passes through:
- **Feasibility study** - technical, economic (cost-benefit), operational, schedule and legal feasibility.
- **Requirements analysis and specification** - output: SRS document.
- **Design** - architecture and module design.
- **Coding and unit testing**.
- **Integration and system testing**.
- **Deployment and maintenance** - usually the longest and costliest phase over the product's life.

A **process model** (life cycle model) fixes the order of these phases and how one moves between them. Umbrella activities such as project tracking, SQA, configuration management, risk management and reviews run throughout.

sections.heading: Process models: waterfall to agile
sections.body:
- **Classical waterfall / linear sequential model** - phases in strict order, each phase finishing before the next. Simple, document-driven, good when requirements are stable; but no working product until late, and it does not cope well with errors or changes left from a previous phase (no feedback paths in the classical form; the *iterative waterfall* adds them).
- **V-model** - waterfall variant pairing each development phase with a testing phase (requirements ↔ acceptance test, design ↔ system/integration test, module design ↔ unit test). Verification on the left arm, validation on the right.
- **Prototyping model** - a quick throwaway prototype clarifies unclear requirements (especially user interface), then the real system is built.
- **Incremental model** - the product is delivered in increments; the first increment is the core product; each release adds features.
- **RAD (Rapid Application Development)** - a **"high-speed" adaptation of the linear sequential model** using component-based construction and code generators; a fully functional system within a short period (about 60-90 days in Pressman) when requirements are well understood and the project can be modularised.
- **Spiral model (Boehm)** - **risk-driven** evolutionary model; each loop of the spiral is a phase with four quadrants: (1) objectives, alternatives, constraints, (2) risk analysis and resolution (often by prototyping), (3) development and verification, (4) planning the next loop. Software is developed in a series of evolutionary/incremental releases. It is called a **meta model** because it subsumes the other models.
- **Evolutionary / iterative**, **concurrent** and **component-based** models; **JAD** (Joint Application Development) uses joint workshops of users and developers.
- **Agile** (Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change). **Scrum**: sprints of 1-4 weeks, product backlog, product owner, Scrum Master, daily stand-up. **XP** (Extreme Programming): pair programming, test-driven development, refactoring, continuous integration, small releases.

sections.heading: Requirements engineering and the SRS
sections.body:
Steps: **elicitation** (interviews, questionnaires, brainstorming, observation, use cases, FAST/JAD sessions) → **analysis** (remove ambiguity, inconsistency, incompleteness) → **specification** (SRS) → **validation** (reviews, prototypes) → management of changes.

- **Functional requirements** - what the system must do (inputs, outputs, functions).
- **Non-functional requirements** - qualities and constraints: performance, reliability, security, usability, portability, maintainability.
- **Domain requirements** - from the application domain.

The **SRS** (Software Requirements Specification, IEEE 830 format) describes **what** the system does, not **how**; it is therefore called a **black-box specification** of the system. A good SRS is correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked for importance, verifiable, modifiable and traceable. It acts as the contract between customer and developer and the basis of acceptance testing.

Analysis modelling tools: **DFD** (data flow diagram; level 0 = **context diagram** showing the whole system as one process), **data dictionary**, **ER diagram**, **decision tables/trees**, **structured English**, **use case diagrams**, **state transition diagrams**.

sections.heading: Software design: modularity, cohesion and coupling
sections.body:
Design principles: **abstraction**, **stepwise refinement** (Wirth, top-down), **modularity**, **information hiding** (Parnas), **functional independence**. Functional independence is measured by **cohesion** (within a module) and **coupling** (between modules). Good design = **high cohesion, low coupling**.

**Cohesion** is a measure of the **functional strength** of a module - how closely its elements belong together. From worst to best:
- **Coincidental** - unrelated tasks grouped arbitrarily.
- **Logical** - elements perform **similar kinds of operations** (e.g. all error handling, all input).
- **Temporal** - executed at the same time (initialisation, shutdown).
- **Procedural** - parts of one algorithm/procedure in sequence.
- **Communicational** - operate on the same data.
- **Sequential** - output of one element is input to the next.
- **Functional** - all elements cooperate to achieve **a single function** (best).

**Coupling** measures the degree of **interdependence** between two modules. From best (loosest) to worst:
- **Data** - communicate through elementary parameters.
- **Stamp** - pass a composite data structure (record).
- **Control** - one passes a flag that controls the other's logic.
- **External** - share an externally imposed format/device (listed by Pressman; not in every text).
- **Common** - share **global data areas**.
- **Content** - one module refers to or changes the internals (code/data) of another (worst).

**Structured partitioning**: the program structure should be partitioned both **horizontally** (separate branches for major functions such as input, processing, output) and **vertically** (factoring: top-level modules make decisions, low-level modules do the work).

**UML** (Unified Modeling Language) diagrams: structural - class, object, component, deployment, package; behavioural - use case, activity, state machine, sequence, communication.

sections.heading: Testing: concepts, levels and types
sections.body:
Testing executes a program to **find errors**; it can show the presence of bugs, never their absence. Boehm's definitions: **Verification** - "Are we building the product **right**?" (conforms to specification; reviews, inspections, walkthroughs). **Validation** - "Are we building the **right** product?" (meets user needs; testing the final product).

**Error** (human mistake) → **fault/defect/bug** (in code) → **failure** (observed wrong behaviour).

**Levels of testing**:
- **Unit testing** - individual modules; needs **drivers** (call the module) and **stubs** (stand in for called modules).
- **Integration testing** - big-bang, **top-down** (uses stubs), **bottom-up** (uses drivers), sandwich/mixed.
- **System testing** - whole system against the SRS: functional, performance (**stress** beyond limits, load, volume), recovery, security, compatibility.
- **Acceptance testing** - by the customer: **alpha** testing at the developer's site with the customer, **beta** testing at customers' sites in a real environment.
- **Regression testing** - re-run tests after changes to ensure nothing broke. **Smoke testing** - quick check that the build is stable enough to test.

**Static techniques** (no execution): **code walkthrough** - an informal team analysis of code, done **after** a module has been coded and compiled; **code inspection** - more formal, checks for classical error types with a checklist; desk checking.

**Debugging approaches**: **brute force** (load the program with print statements / memory dumps and hope the values reveal the error - least efficient, most common), **backtracking** (trace backwards from the symptom), **cause elimination** (induction/deduction, binary partitioning of hypotheses).

sections.heading: Black-box and white-box test design
sections.body:
**Black-box testing** (functional / behavioural) designs tests from the specification only:
- **Equivalence partitioning** - divide inputs into classes expected to behave alike; pick one value from each valid and invalid class.
- **Boundary value analysis (BVA)** - errors cluster at boundaries, so test at and just beyond them. For a range [min, max], Rajib Mall's rule picks min−1, min, max, max+1; robust BVA (Jorgensen) also uses min+1, a nominal value and max−1.
- **Cause-effect graphing**, **decision-table testing**, **state-transition testing**.

**White-box testing** (also called **glass-box**, structural or clear-box testing) designs tests from the code:
- **Statement coverage** (every statement once) < **branch/decision coverage** (each branch true and false) < **path coverage**; condition and MC/DC coverage.
- **Basis path testing** (McCabe): the number of independent paths = **cyclomatic complexity V(G)**, which is also an upper bound on tests needed for branch coverage.
- **Loop testing** (simple, nested, concatenated loops), **data-flow testing** (definition-use pairs), **mutation testing** (small changes 'mutants' must be detected by the test suite).

**Cyclomatic complexity** of a control flow graph with E edges, N nodes and P connected components: **V(G) = E − N + 2P** (= E − N + 2 for one program); also V(G) = number of **decision (predicate) nodes + 1** = number of **regions** of a planar flow graph.

sections.heading: Project management and size metrics
sections.body:
**Management functions**: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling. The project manager's key jobs: estimation, scheduling, staffing, **risk management**, configuration management, monitoring and control.

**Estimation techniques** (Rajib Mall's classification): **empirical** (expert judgement, **Delphi**), **heuristic** (models such as COCOMO), **analytical** (e.g. **Halstead's software science**). Prototyping is not an estimation technique.

**Size metrics**:
- **LOC / KLOC** - simple but language-dependent and known only late.
- **Function Points (FP)** (Albrecht) - language-independent, from the SRS. Count five parameters - External Inputs (EI), External Outputs (EO), External Inquiries (EQ), Internal Logical Files (ILF), External Interface Files (EIF) - each weighted simple/average/complex to get the **Unadjusted FP (UFP)**. Fourteen general system characteristics, each rated 0-5, give **VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ** (range 0.65 to 1.35), and **FP = UFP × VAF**.

**Software metrics** (Pressman): **direct measures** of the product include LOC, execution speed, memory size and defects reported; **indirect measures** include functionality, quality, complexity, efficiency, reliability and maintainability.

**Risk management**: identify → analyse (probability and impact; **risk exposure RE = P × C**) → plan (avoid, transfer, mitigate) → monitor (RMMM plan). Risk categories: project, technical, business risks.

sections.heading: COCOMO, PERT, CPM and Gantt charts
sections.body:
**COCOMO** (Constructive Cost Model, Boehm, 1981) estimates effort from size. Project classes: **organic** (small team, familiar problem), **semi-detached** (mixed experience), **embedded** (tight hardware/real-time constraints). Three levels: **basic**, **intermediate** (multiplies by an Effort Adjustment Factor from 15 cost drivers) and **detailed/complete** (phase-wise). COCOMO II is the later revision.

Basic COCOMO: **Effort E = a × (KLOC)ᵇ person-months**, **Development time D = c × Eᵈ months**, average staff = E ÷ D.

**Scheduling tools**:
- **Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)** - hierarchical decomposition of the project into tasks.
- **Activity network / CPM** - activities with durations and dependencies; the **critical path** is the longest path; it fixes the minimum project duration and its activities have zero slack.
- **PERT** (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) - a network of boxes and arrows in which the **boxes represent activities and the arrows represent task dependencies**; it uses three time estimates (optimistic o, most likely m, pessimistic p). Expected time tₑ = (o + 4m + p) ÷ 6, standard deviation σ = (p − o) ÷ 6.
- **Gantt chart** - bar chart of activities against time, useful for resource planning and tracking. A Gantt chart **can be derived automatically from a PERT chart**, but a PERT chart **cannot be derived from a Gantt chart** because a Gantt chart lacks dependency information.
- **Project management software** (e.g. MS Project) provides scheduling, resource allocation, task lists and communication features.

sections.heading: Maintenance, re-engineering and configuration management
sections.body:
**Software maintenance** = modifying software after delivery. Types:
- **Corrective** - fix reported faults.
- **Adaptive** - adapt to a changed environment (new OS, hardware, laws).
- **Perfective** - add features or improve performance on user request (usually the largest share).
- **Preventive** - improve future maintainability (restructuring, documentation).

**Lehman's laws** of software evolution: a used program must **continually change** or become less useful; as it evolves its **complexity increases** unless work is done to reduce it. Software evolution has several aspects, including the software architecture aspect and the programming language aspect.

- **Reverse engineering** - recovering the design and requirements specification of a product from an analysis of its code.
- **Re-engineering** = reverse engineering + restructuring + forward engineering; used for **legacy systems**.
- **Software Configuration Management (SCM)** - identification of configuration items, **baselines**, version control, change control, configuration audits and status reporting.
- **CASE tools** (Computer Aided Software Engineering) automate SDLC activities: **upper CASE** (analysis, design: DFD/UML editors), **lower CASE** (code generation, testing, debugging). They improve quality and productivity, reduce drudgery and lower maintenance cost.

sections.heading: Software quality, SQA and reliability
sections.body:
**SQA** (Software Quality Assurance) is an umbrella activity: standards, reviews, audits, testing, measurement and reporting to ensure the process and product meet quality requirements. **Quality control** checks products; **quality assurance** checks the process.

- **McCall's quality factors**: product operation (correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity, usability), product revision (maintainability, flexibility, testability), product transition (portability, reusability, interoperability).
- **ISO 9001** - quality management standard applicable to software organisations; **ISO/IEC 9126**, later **ISO/IEC 25010** - product quality models.
- **SEI CMM** (Capability Maturity Model) levels: **1 Initial** (ad hoc) → **2 Repeatable** (basic project management) → **3 Defined** (documented organisation-wide process) → **4 Managed** (quantitative measurement) → **5 Optimizing** (continuous process improvement). CMMI is its integrated successor.
- **Six Sigma** - at most 3.4 defects per million opportunities.

**Reliability metrics**:
- **ROCOF** - Rate of Occurrence of Failure.
- **MTTF** - Mean Time To Failure; **MTTR** - Mean Time To Repair; **MTBF = MTTF + MTTR** (Mean Time Between Failures).
- **POFOD** - Probability of Failure On Demand.
- **Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR)**.

**Halstead's software science** uses operators and operands: n₁, n₂ distinct operators/operands, N₁, N₂ total occurrences; vocabulary n = n₁ + n₂, length N = N₁ + N₂, volume V = N log₂ n.

formulas.name: Cyclomatic complexity
formulas.formula: V(G) = E − N + 2P  = predicates + 1 = number of regions
formulas.note: P = connected components (1 for a single program).

formulas.name: Basic COCOMO time
formulas.note: d = 0.38 organic, 0.35 semi-detached, 0.32 embedded; staff = E ÷ D.

formulas.name: PERT expected time
formulas.note: o optimistic, m most likely, p pessimistic.

formulas.name: Availability
formulas.formula: A = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR);  MTBF = MTTF + MTTR

formulas.name: Risk exposure
formulas.note: P = probability of the risk, C = cost/impact if it occurs.

formulas.name: Halstead volume
formulas.formula: V = N × log₂ n,  n = n₁ + n₂,  N = N₁ + N₂

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A project of 32 KLOC is classified as organic. Using basic COCOMO estimate effort, development time and average staff.
workedExamples.solution:
Organic: a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38.
- Effort E = 2.4 × 32¹·⁰⁵. Since 32¹·⁰⁵ ≈ 38.05, E ≈ 2.4 × 38.05 ≈ **91.3 person-months**.
- Time D = 2.5 × 91.3⁰·³⁸. 91.3⁰·³⁸ ≈ 5.56, so D ≈ **13.9 months**.
- Average staff = 91.3 ÷ 13.9 ≈ **6.6, i.e. about 7 persons**.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A system has 20 EI, 12 EO, 8 EQ, 4 ILF and 2 EIF, all of average complexity. The 14 complexity adjustment factors add up to 42. Find the function points.
Find the cyclomatic complexity of function f() in the white-box section by all three methods.
workedExamples.solution:
Nodes N1-N9 (9 nodes). Edges: N1→N2, N2→N3, N2→N7, N3→N4, N3→N5, N4→N6, N5→N6, N6→N2, N7→N8, N7→N9, N8→N9 = 11 edges.
- V(G) = E − N + 2 = 11 − 9 + 2 = **4**.
- Predicates: while (n > 0), if (n % 2 == 0), if (s > 10) → 3 + 1 = **4**.
- Regions: three enclosed regions (if-else diamond, loop, final if) + the outer region = **4**.
So at least 4 independent paths must be tested. Check of the output: f(3): n=3 → s=−1, n=2 → s=1, n=1 → s=0 → returns 0; f(4) → 4−1+2−1 = 4; f(8) gives 8−1+6−1+4−1+2−1 = 16 > 10 → 10. Output `0 4 10`.

workedExamples.problem: A field accepts integer marks from 1 to 100. Give equivalence classes and boundary-value test inputs.
workedExamples.solution:
Equivalence classes: one valid class 1-100; two invalid classes: below 1 (≤ 0) and above 100 (≥ 101). Representatives e.g. 50, −5, 150.
Boundary values (Mall's rule: min−1, min, max, max+1): **0, 1, 100, 101**.
Robust BVA (adds just-inside values and a nominal value): 0, 1, 2, 50, 99, 100, 101.

workedExamples.problem: Activities (days): A=3 (start), B=4 after A, C=2 after A, D=5 after B, E=6 after C, F=2 after D and E. Find the critical path, project duration and slack of C. Also, for an activity with o=4, m=7, p=16, find the PERT expected time and σ.
workedExamples.solution:
Paths: A-B-D-F = 3+4+5+2 = **14 days**; A-C-E-F = 3+2+6+2 = 13 days.
Critical path = **A-B-D-F**, duration 14 days. Slack on C (and E) = 14 − 13 = **1 day**.
PERT: tₑ = (4 + 4×7 + 16) ÷ 6 = 48 ÷ 6 = **8 days**; σ = (16 − 4) ÷ 6 = **2 days**.

workedExamples.problem: A server has MTTF = 480 hours and MTTR = 20 hours. Find MTBF and availability.

pitfalls: Linear sequential model = waterfall; RAD is the 'high-speed' adaptation of the linear sequential model.
Spiral model is risk-driven and is called a meta model; it is evolutionary, not purely sequential.
Cohesion = functional strength within a module (want high); coupling = interdependence between modules (want low).
Logical cohesion = similar operations (all error handling); functional cohesion = one single function.
Common coupling = shared global data; content coupling (worst) = one module touches another's internals.
White-box testing is also called glass-box testing; equivalence partitioning and BVA are black-box methods.
V(G) = E − N + 2, not E + N − 2 or E − N − 2.
Verification: building the product right; validation: building the right product.
The SRS is a black-box specification: it says what, not how.
A Gantt chart can be derived from a PERT chart, not the other way round.
Code walkthrough is informal and done after coding a module, not before.
ROCOF = rate of occurrence of failure; MTTF = mean time to failure.
quickRevision: Software is developed, not manufactured, and does not wear out.
Waterfall = linear sequential = classic life cycle model.
Spiral model (Boehm): four quadrants, risk analysis each loop, 'meta model'.
SRS standard: IEEE 830; context diagram = level-0 DFD.
Cohesion order: coincidental < logical < temporal < procedural < communicational < sequential < functional.
Coupling order: data < stamp < control < (external) < common < content.
Stubs replace called modules (top-down); drivers call the module under test (bottom-up).
Alpha test at developer site; beta test at customer site.
Brute-force debugging = print statements / memory dumps.
FP: 5 parameters (EI, EO, EQ, ILF, EIF) and 14 adjustment factors.
COCOMO classes: organic, semi-detached, embedded; levels: basic, intermediate, detailed.
Maintenance types: corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive.
CMM levels: Initial, Repeatable, Defined, Managed, Optimizing.
CASE = Computer Aided Software Engineering; SQA = Software Quality Assurance.
